newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel sidelined, German tax row rages on.
newsitem.headline: Waigel sidelined, German tax row rages on.

text.p: Germany began the most crucial week of its budget year on Monday with Finance Minister Theo Waigel sidelined by illness and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's party calling the opposition's bluff over a blockade of the 1997 tax bill.

Waigel has been under enormous pressure in recent weeks to plug gaps in state finances next year and conjure a budget which meets the strict borrowing limits required to qualify for European monetary union.
That pressure looked finally to have caught up with the 57-year-old minister, who took to his bed with a cold after his Christian Social Union's (CSU) annual party conference on Saturday.

A spokesman said Waigel would not return to the fray until Thursday -- the day before the final reading and vote in the Bundestag lower house of parliament on his ninth budget. He has been ordered to stay in bed by his doctors until then.

Waigel often appears to have been carrying the torch of budget austerity alone amid attacks from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and even the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), partners in Kohl's 14-year, three-party coalition.

Rows with the FDP over cutting the solidarity surcharge, an unpopular tax levied to help finance the reconstruction of former communist east Germany, have been put on ice until December. But the coalition still looks unstable on the issue.
Newspaper reports at the weekend that Kohl was floating the idea of bringing forward a major tax-cutting reform to 1998, an election year, were denied on Monday by CDU officials.
CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said that, apart from a cut in the solidarity tax -- whose size has yet to be agreed -- there would be no other major tax cuts in 1998.
Meanwhile, FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said on Monday that elements of the tax reform should take effect as soon as possible "to give investors in Germany more air to breathe."

More pressing for now is a standoff between the government and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) over the 1997 tax bill. The SPD has used its blocking majority in the Bundesrat upper house to force a showdown over the abolition of wealth and property dealing taxes.
"These taxes must go," Hintze told reporters.

Failure to agree a compromise would mean that the wealth tax -- ruled illegal by the constitutional court -- would be scrapped next year. That, Hintze said, would make the SPD responsible for a major loss of government revenue.
Germany's constitution requires a compromise to be reached between the two houses of parliament if tax legislation is rejected by the Bundesrat.

If no deal is reached that could again throw Waigel's budget calculations into turmoil -- just as Germany is urging fiscal discipline on Italy following the readmission of the lira to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) at the weekend.
ERM membership is a stepping stone to joining the launch of the single currency, scheduled for 1999.

At the moment Waigel's 1997 total public sector budget deficit is projected at 99 billion marks -- equivalent to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product. The Maastricht deficit ceiling is three percent.
